identity.name: Republic of Cuba in Arms (Ten Years' War)
alt_names: Republic in Arms of the Ten Years' War
First Republic of Cuba in Arms

land.text: Oriente, where 'On 10 October 1868, sugar mill owner Carlos Manuel de Céspedes and his followers proclaimed independence'

predecessors.note: The Spanish colony of Cuba (Captaincy General of Cuba) is the immediate counterpart; Cliopatria's Kingdom of Spain row is the nearest shape.

land.text: the eastern provinces, where the war resumed in 1895 as the second Republic in Arms (Cliopatria 'Cuban Nationalists', 1895-1899)

successors.note: The Pact of Zanjón of 10 February 1878 returned the east to Spanish rule; the Little War of 1879-80 and the 1895 insurrection are separate. Same Wikipedia page, a different state in Cliopatria.

rulers.name: Carlos Manuel de Céspedes
rulers.note: Elected President of the Republic in Arms on 12 April 1869; removed in 1873; killed on 27 February 1874 (Ten Years' War page).

rulers.name: Salvador Cisneros Betancourt
rulers.note: Assumed the presidency on 27 October 1873; replaced by Spotorno in July 1875.

rulers.name: Tomás Estrada Palma
rulers.note: President from 29 March 1876; captured by Spanish forces in 1877.

rulers.name: García González
rulers.note: The page says only that "García González's term ended with the signing of the" Pact of Zanjón on 10 February 1878; the start (after 13 December 1877) is the researcher's reading and the first name is not on the page.

correction.text: Oriente, where the uprising began in October 1868 and where the rebels 'seized the important city of Bayamo'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, Cliopatria's Cuban Nationalists row is 1895-1899 only. The page gives no extent for 1868; Oriente is the researcher's reading. No area on either page.

correction.text: Oriente and Camagüey: 'on 4 November 1868, Camagüey rose up in arms during the Las Clavellinas Uprising'; the republic 'divided Cuba into four military regions: Oriente, Camagüey, Las Villas and Occidente'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The pages say the uprising reached Las Villas in February 1869 and 'was not supported in the westernmost provinces of Pinar del Río, Havana and Matanzas'; control is not described, so the held zone is the eastern two regions and Las Villas is a contest zone (ledger). The page gives a population of 1,509,291 for Cuba in the 1877 census, not an area; the gazetteer resolves all of Cuba to about 128,200 km2.

region.text: Oriente: 'Carlos Manuel de Céspedes and his followers proclaimed independence'

ledger.note: 10 October 1868: Céspedes proclaims Cuban independence (the Grito de Yara). 'On 10 October 1868, sugar mill owner Carlos Manuel de Céspedes and his followers proclaimed independence.' The page names Oriente, not a boundary.

region.text: the important city of Bayamo, seized 'after three days of combat'

ledger.note: October 1868: the rebels seize Bayamo. 'After three days of combat, the rebels seized the important city of Bayamo.' The page gives no day; the Spanish retook it on 12 January 1869.

region.text: Camagüey: 'on 4 November 1868, Camagüey rose up in arms during the Las Clavellinas Uprising'

ledger.note: 4 November 1868: Camagüey rises in arms (Las Clavellinas Uprising). The page says the province rose; it does not say the rebels held it, so this is the researcher's reading of control.

region.text: Bayamo, retaken by the Spanish on 12 January

ledger.note: 12 January 1869: the Spanish retake Bayamo. The page says only 'The Spanish retook it on 12 January'; the year is by context.

region.text: Las Villas: 'in early February 1869, Las Villas followed'

ledger.note: February 1869: Las Villas rises. 'in early February 1869, Las Villas followed'; the rising 'was not supported in the westernmost provinces of Pinar del Río, Havana and Matanzas'.

10 April 1869: the Assembly of Guáimaro adopts the first Constitution of Cuba. 'On April 10, 1869 ... the first Constitution of Cuba was adopted'; on 12 April Céspedes is elected president of the Republic in Arms. The rising becomes a republic; same state, colour continues.
10 February 1878: the Pact of Zanjón ends the war. 'it was signed on 10 February 1878, by a negotiating committee'; the Baraguá protest followed on 15 March; infobox end 28 May 1878.

region.text: the rebel east, returned to Spanish rule by the Pact of Zanjón

ledger.note: 10 February 1878: the Republic in Arms ends at Zanjón. 'On February 10, 1878, García González's term ended with the signing of the' Pact of Zanjón, 'which ended the Ten Years' War'.

region.text: the Republic in Arms of the Ten Years' War

ledger.note: February 1878: the first Republic in Arms ends. Pact of Zanjón of 10 February 1878; the war's infobox end is 28 May 1878.

wars.name: Ten Years' War
wars.outcome: Spanish victory: the Pact of Zanjón of 10 February 1878; Céspedes killed on 27 February 1874; Baraguá protest 15 March 1878; infobox '10 October 1868 – 28 May 1878'.
wars.note: Spanish trochas are not mentioned on the page. The western provinces of Pinar del Río, Havana and Matanzas did not rise.

certainty.note: Guerrilla war: no frontier is described and the republic held no stable territory the pages name.

sources.title: Ten Years' War
sources.note: Grito de Yara 10 October 1868, Bayamo, Camagüey 4 November 1868, Las Villas February 1869, Guáimaro 10 April 1869, Zanjón 10 February 1878.

sources.title: Republic of Cuba in Arms
sources.note: Guáimaro constitution, presidents 1869-1877, four military regions, Zanjón; the page's later section is the 1895 republic (already the cuban-nationalists dossier).

notes:
Cliopatria's Cuban Nationalists row covers 1895-1899 only; the am-08-h dossier cuban-nationalists names the 1869-1878 Republic in Arms as outside its row. This dossier writes that first period as its own state, with cuban-nationalists as its (spiritual) successor. Same Wikipedia page, so the colour agent can share the family and may choose to share the colour.
Counterpart: kingdom-of-spain, as the cuban-nationalists dossier does; captaincy-general-of-cuba (written in this batch) is the colony itself.
Thin: the pages never say which towns the rebels held after Bayamo, give no capital or area, and the Little War of 1879-80 is not covered. The 'held' zone (Oriente and Camagüey provinces in modern boundaries) is the researcher's reading and an upper bound.
